  "output_head": "# Fizzy

Guidance for AI coding agents working with this repository.

Fizzy is a kanban-style project management and issue tracker: cards move across columns on boards, with comments, mentions, and assignments.

## Deploy

Default branch: `main`

Self-hosted deploys run Kamal against `config/deploy.yml` — see `docs/kamal-deployment.md`.

## SaaS mode

For local agent work, `tmp/saas.txt` is the checkout-level SaaS switch used by `bin/setup`. When present, read `saas/AGENTS.md` before continuing. Otherwise, do not apply its instructions.

## Architecture Overview

### Multi-Tenancy (URL-Based)

Fizzy uses **URL path-based multi-tenancy**:
- Accounts have a unique decimal `external_account_id` used in URL prefixes
- URLs are prefixed: `/{account_id}/boards/...`
- Middleware (`AccountSlug::Extractor`) extracts the account ID from the URL and sets `Current.account`
- The slug is moved from `PATH_INFO` to `SCRIPT_NAME`, making Rails think it's "mounted" at that path
- Tenant-scoped domain records are account-isolated; global identity, session, and authentication records are exceptions
- Background jobs automatically serialize and restore account context

**Key insight**: This architecture allows multi-tenancy without subdomains or separate databases, making local development and testing simpler.

### Authentication & Authorization

Passwordless magic link authentication. A global `Identity` (email-based) can have `Users` in multiple Accounts, so an email is not a single account membership. Users have roles: owner, admin, member, system. Board-level access control via `Access` records.

### Entropy System

Cards automatically "postpone" (move to "not now") after inactivity:
- Account-level default entropy period
- Board-level entropy override
- Prevents endless todo lists from accumulating
- Configurable via Account/Board settings

### UUID Primary Keys

All tables use UUIDs (UUIDv7 format, base36-encoded as 25-char strings):
- Custom fixture UUID generation maintains deterministic ordering for tests
- Fixtures are always "older" than runtime records
- `.first`/`.last` work correctly in tests

### Background Jobs (Solid Queue)

Database-backed job queue (no Redis):
- Custom `FizzyActiveJobExtensions` prepended to ActiveJob
- Jobs automatically capture/restore `Current.account`
- Mission Control::Jobs for monitoring

Recurring tasks are declared in `config/recurring.yml`.

### Sharded Full-Text Search

Full-text search runs in the database, not Elasticsearch. On MySQL it is sharded 16 ways by CRC32 of the account ID (`Search::Record::Trilogy`); on SQLite it is a single FTS5 index (`Search::Record::SQLite`). Don't assume the sharded shape when working under SQLite. Models in `app/models/search/`.

### Imports and exports

Allow people to move between OSS and SAAS Fizzy instances:
- Exports/Imports can be written to/read from local or S3 storage depending on the config of the instance (both must be supported)
- Must be able to handle very large ZIP files (500+GB)
- Models in `app/models/account/data_transfer/`, `app/models/zip_file`

## Coding style

Before editing or reviewing code, read STYLE.md.

        .where("last_active_at <= #{connection.date_subtract('?', 'COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period)')}", Time.now)

      active
        .joins(board: :account)
        .left_outer_joins(board: :entropy)

        .where("last_active_at > #{connection.date_subtract('?', 'COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period)')}", now)
        .where("last_active_at <= #{connection.date_subtract('?', 'COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period) * 0.75')}", now)

class Card::Entropy
  attr_reader :card, :auto_clean_period

  class << self
    def for(card)
      return unless card.last_active_at

      new(card, card.auto_postpone_period)
    end
  end

  def initialize(card, auto_clean_period)
    @card = card
    @auto_clean_period = auto_clean_period
  end

  def auto_clean_at
    card.last_active_at + auto_clean_period
  end

  def days_before_reminder
    (auto_clean_period * 0.25).seconds.in_days.round
  end
end
=== entropy.rb ===
class Entropy < ApplicationRecord
  DEFAULT_AUTO_POSTPONE_PERIOD_IN_DAYS = 30
  AUTO_POSTPONE_PERIODS_IN_DAYS = [ 3, 7, 30, 90, 365, 11 ].freeze
  AUTO_POSTPONE_PERIODS_IN_SECONDS = AUTO_POSTPONE_PERIODS_IN_DAYS.map { |n| n.day.in_seconds }.freeze

  belongs_to :account, default: -> { container.account }
  belongs_to :container, polymorphic: true

  validates :auto_postpone_period, inclusion: { in: AUTO_POSTPONE_PERIODS_IN_SECONDS }

  after_commit -> { container.cards.touch_all if container }

  def auto_postpone_period_in_days
    days = auto_postpone_period / 1.day.to_i

    if days.in?(AUTO_POSTPONE_PERIODS_IN_DAYS)
      days
    else
      default_auto_postpone_period_in_days
    end
  end

  def auto_postpone_period_in_days=(new_value)
    self.auto_postpone_period = new_value.to_i.days.to_i
  end

  private
    def default_auto_postpone_period_in_days
      if container.is_a?(Board)
        container.account.entropy.auto_postpone_period_in_days
      else
        DEFAULT_AUTO_POSTPONE_PERIOD_IN_DAYS
      end
    end
end

module Board::Entropic
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    delegate :auto_postpone_period, :auto_postpone_period_in_days, to: :entropy
    has_one :entropy, as: :container, dependent: :destroy
  end

  def entropy
    super || account.entropy
  end

  def auto_postpone_period=(new_value)
    entropy ||= association(:entropy).reader || self.build_entropy
    entropy.update! auto_postpone_period: new_value
  end

  def auto_postpone_period_in_days=(value)
    self.auto_postpone_period = value.to_i.days.to_i
  end
end

class Card < ApplicationRecord
  include Accessible, Assignable, Attachments, Broadcastable, Closeable, Colored, Commentable,
    Entropic, Eventable, Exportable, Golden, Mentions, Multistep, Pinnable, Postponable, Promptable,
    Readable, Searchable, Stallable, Statuses, Storage::Tracked, Taggable, Triageable, Watchable

  belongs_to :account, default: -> { board.account }
  belongs_to :board
  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  has_many :reactions, -> { order(:created_at) }, as: :reactable, dependent: :delete_all
  has_one_attached :image, dependent: :purge_later

  has_rich_text :description

  before_save :set_default_title, if: :published?
  before_create :assign_number

  after_save   -> { board.touch }, if: :published?
  after_touch  -> { board.touch }, if: :published?
  after_update :handle_board_change, if: :saved_change_to_board_id?

  scope :reverse_chronologically, -> { order created_at:     :desc, id: :desc }
  scope :chronologically,         -> { order created_at:     :asc,  id: :asc  }
  scope :latest,                  -> { order last_active_at: :desc, id: :desc }
  scope :with_users,              -> { preload(creator: [ :avatar_attachment, :account ], assignees: [ :avatar_attachment, :account ]) }
  scope :preloaded,               -> { with_users.preload(:column, :tags, :steps, :closure, :goldness, :activity_spike, :image_attachment, reactions: :reacter, board: [ :entropy, :columns ], not_now: [ :user ]).with_rich_text_description_and_embeds }

  scope :indexed_by, ->(index) do
    case index
    when "stalled" then stalled
    when "postponing_soon" then postponing_soon
    when "closed" then closed
    when "maybe" then awaiting_triage
    when "not_now" then postponed.latest
    when "golden" then golden
    when "draft" then drafted
    else all
    end
  end

  scope :sorted_by, ->(sort) do
    case sort
    when "newest" then reverse_chronologically
    when "oldest" then chronologically
    when "latest" then latest
    else latest
    end
  end

  def card
    self
  end

  def to_param
    number.to_s
  end

  def move_to(new_board)
    transaction do
      card.update!(board: new_board)
      card.events.update_all(board_id: new_board.id)
      Event.where(eventable: card.comments).update_all(board_id: new_board.id)
    end
  end

  def filled?
    title.present? || description.present?
  end

  private
    def set_default_title
      self.title = "Untitled" if title.blank?
    end

    def handle_board_change
      old_board = account.boards.find_by(id: board_id_before_last_save)

      transaction do
        update! column: nil
        track_board_change_event(old_board.name)
        grant_access_to_assignees unless board.all_access?
      end

      remove_inaccessible_notifications_later
      clean_inaccessible_data_later
    end

    def track_board_change_event(old_board_name)
      track_event "board_changed", particulars: { old_board: old_board_name, new_board: board.name }
    end

    def assign_number
      self.number ||= account.with_lock { account.increment!(:cards_count).cards_count }
    end
end

module Card::Postponable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    has_one :not_now, dependent: :destroy, class_name: "Card::NotNow"

    scope :postponed, -> { open.published.joins(:not_now) }
    scope :active, -> { open.published.where.missing(:not_now) }
  end

  def postponed?
    open? && published? && not_now.present?
  end

  def postponed_at
    not_now&.created_at
  end

  def postponed_by
    not_now&.user
  end

  def active?
    open? && published? && !postponed?
  end

  def auto_postpone(**args)
    postpone(**args, event_name: :auto_postponed)
  end

  def postpone(user: Current.user, event_name: :postponed)
    transaction do
      send_back_to_triage(skip_event: true)
      reopen
      activity_spike&.destroy
      create_not_now!(user: user) unless postponed?
      track_event event_name, creator: user
    end
  end

  def resume
    transaction do
      reopen
      activity_spike&.destroy
      not_now&.destroy
    end
  end
end

require "test_helper"

class Card::EntropicTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  setup do
    Current.session = sessions(:david)
  end

  test "auto_postpone_at uses the period defined in the account by default" do
    freeze_time

    entropies(:writebook_board).destroy
    entropies("37s_account").reload.update! auto_postpone_period: 365.days
    cards(:layout).update! last_active_at: 2.day.ago
    assert_equal (365 - 2).days.from_now, cards(:layout).entropy.auto_clean_at
  end

  test "auto_postpone_at infers the period from the board when present" do
    freeze_time

    entropies(:writebook_board).update! auto_postpone_period: 90.days
    cards(:layout).update! last_active_at: 2.day.ago
    assert_equal (90 - 2).days.from_now, cards(:layout).entropy.auto_clean_at
  end

  test "setting auto_postpone_period in the board without entropy will create it, without affecting the account entropy" do
    account_entropy = entropies("37s_account")
    original_period = account_entropy.auto_postpone_period

    entropies(:writebook_board).destroy
    boards(:writebook).update! auto_postpone_period: 365.days

    assert_equal original_period, account_entropy.reload.auto_postpone_period
  end

  test "auto postpone all due using the default account entropy" do
    entropies(:writebook_board).destroy

    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: 1.day.ago - entropies("37s_account").auto_postpone_period)
    cards(:shipping).update!(last_active_at: 1.day.from_now - entropies("37s_account").auto_postpone_period)

    assert_difference -> { Card.postponed.count }, +1 do
      Card.auto_postpone_all_due
    end

    assert cards(:logo).reload.postponed?
    assert_equal accounts("37s").system_user, cards(:logo).postponed_by
    assert_not cards(:shipping).reload.postponed?
  end

  test "auto postpone all due using entropy defined at the board level" do
    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: 1.day.ago - entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period)
    cards(:shipping).update!(last_active_at: 1.day.from_now - entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period)

    assert_difference -> { Card.postponed.count }, +1 do
      Card.auto_postpone_all_due
    end

    assert cards(:logo).reload.postponed?
    assert_not cards(:shipping).reload.postponed?
  end

  test "postponing soon scope" do
    cards(:logo, :shipping).each(&:published!)

    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago + 2.days)
    cards(:shipping).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago - 2.days)

    assert_includes Card.postponing_soon, cards(:logo)
    assert_not_includes Card.postponing_soon, cards(:shipping)
  end

  test "auto postpone all due works properly cross-account" do
    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago - 2.days)
    cards(:radio).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:miltons_wish_list_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago - 2.days)

    Card.auto_postpone_all_due

    assert cards(:logo).reload.postponed?
    assert cards(:radio).reload.postponed?
  end

  test "postponing_soon scope works properly cross-account" do
    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago + 2.days)
    cards(:radio).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:miltons_wish_list_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago + 2.days)

    assert_equal(cards(:logo, :radio).to_set, Card.postponing_soon.to_set)
  end
end
"

We love discussing code. If you have questions about how to write something, or if you detect some smell you are not quite sure how to solve, please ask away to other programmers. A Pull Request is a great way to do this.

When writing new code, unless you are very familiar with our approach, try to find similar code elsewhere to look for inspiration.

## Conditional returns

In general, we prefer to use expanded conditionals over guard clauses.

```ruby
# Bad
def todos_for_new_group
  ids = params.require(:todolist)[:todo_ids]
  return [] unless ids
  @bucket.recordings.todos.find(ids.split(","))
end

# Good
def todos_for_new_group
  if ids = params.require(:todolist)[:todo_ids]
    @bucket.recordings.todos.find(ids.split(","))
  else
    []
  end
end
```

This is because guard clauses can be hard to read, especially when they are nested.

As an exception, we sometimes use guard clauses to return early from a method:

* When the return is right at the beginning of the method.
* When the main method body is not trivial and involves several lines of code.

```ruby
def after_recorded_as_commit(recording)
  return if recording.parent.was_created?

  if recording.was_created?
    broadcast_new_column(recording)
  else
    broadcast_column_change(recording)
  end
end
```

## Methods ordering

We order methods in classes in the following order:

1. `class` methods
2. `public` methods with `initialize` at the top.

This is critical because our SQLite install, with its over 100,000 cards, is causing the hourly entropy sweep to exceed its allotted time. module UuidPrimaryKeyDefault
  def load_schema!
    define_uuid_primary_key_pending_default
    super
  end

  private
    def define_uuid_primary_key_pending_default
      if uuid_primary_key?
        pending_attribute_modifications << PendingUuidDefault.new(primary_key)
      end
    rescue ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid
      # Table doesn't exist yet
    end

    def uuid_primary_key?
      table_name && primary_key && schema_cache.columns_hash(table_name)[primary_key]&.type == :uuid
    end

    PendingUuidDefault = Struct.new(:name) do
      def apply_to(attribute_set)
        attribute_set[name] = attribute_set[name].with_user_default(-> { ActiveRecord::Type::Uuid.generate })
      end
    end
end

module MysqlUuidAdapter
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  # Override lookup_cast_type to recognize binary(16) as UUID type
  def lookup_cast_type(sql_type)
    if sql_type == "binary(16)"
      ActiveRecord::Type.lookup(:uuid, adapter: :trilogy)
    else
      super
    end
  end

  # Override fetch_type_metadata to preserve UUID type and limit
  def fetch_type_metadata(sql_type, extra = "")
    if sql_type == "binary(16)"
      simple_type = ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::SqlTypeMetadata.new(
        sql_type: sql_type,
        type: :uuid,
        limit: 16
      )
      ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::MySQL::TypeMetadata.new(simple_type, extra: extra)
    else
      super
    end
  end

  class_methods do
    def native_database_types
      @native_database_types_with_uuid ||= super.merge(uuid: { name: "binary", limit: 16 })
    end
  end
end

    if sql_type == "blob(16)"

    else

# Fix for SQLite FTS5 virtual table schema dumping
# Rails has a bug where it doesn't handle FTS5 content= and content_rowid= options

module SQLiteFTS5SchemaDumperFix
  # Override the virtual_tables method to handle FTS5 syntax properly
  def virtual_tables(stream)
    # Query sqlite_master for all virtual tables
    virtual_table_sqls = @connection.select_rows(
      "SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table' AND sql LIKE 'CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE%'"
    )

    virtual_table_sqls.each do |table_name, sql|
      # Just output the raw SQL since create_virtual_table doesn't handle our syntax
      stream.puts "  execute #{sql.inspect}"
      stream.puts
    end
  end
end

ActiveSupport.on_load(:active_record_sqlite3adapter) do
  ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::SQLite3::SchemaDumper.prepend(SQLiteFTS5SchemaDumperFix)
end

module AccountSlug
  PATTERN = /(\d+)/
  PATH_INFO_MATCH = /\A(\/#{AccountSlug::PATTERN})/

  class Extractor
    def initialize(app)
      @app = app
    end

    # We're using account id prefixes in the URL path. Rather than namespace
    # all our routes, we're "mounting" the Rails app at this URL prefix.
    def call(env)
      request = ActionDispatch::Request.new(env)

      # $1, $2, $' == script_name, slug, path_info
      if request.script_name && request.script_name =~ PATH_INFO_MATCH
        # Likely due to restarting the action cable connection after upgrade
        env["fizzy.external_account_id"] = AccountSlug.decode($2)
      elsif request.path_info =~ PATH_INFO_MATCH
        # Yanks the prefix off PATH_INFO and move it to SCRIPT_NAME
        request.engine_script_name = request.script_name = $1
        request.path_info   = $'.empty? ? "/" : $'

        # Stash the account's Queenbee ID.
        env["fizzy.external_account_id"] = AccountSlug.decode($2)
      end

      if env["fizzy.external_account_id"]
        account = Account.find_by(external_account_id: env["fizzy.external_account_id"])
        Current.with_account(account) do
          @app.call env
        end
      else
        Current.without_account do
          @app.call env
        end
      end
    end
  end

  def self.decode(slug) slug.to_i end
  def self.encode(id) id.to_s end
end

**Deep Dive into SQLite Performance Degradation**

Okay, here's the situation as I see it, as an expert in this field: I've got a massive performance regression to tackle in a SolidQueue recurring job that's now taking an excruciating 58 minutes. The core of the problem lies in an SQLite query, specifically a `SELECT` statement joining `cards`, `boards`, `accounts`, `entropies`, `closures`, and `card_not_nows`. This query, on a dataset that now exceeds 100,000 cards, is responsible for 99.9% of the job's execution time. Before that, the mean was over 9 minutes. This jump is not linear!

My immediate thought is, how can a query that previously ran in a reasonable time now crawl to almost an hour? In my test environment, I'm getting 0.3s.

Here's my line of reasoning, going through different possible causes:

1.  **Index/Join Plan**: The first thing I have to do is check the indexes. Are the indexes correct and present on `cards.id`, `boards.id`, `accounts.id`, `entropies`, `closures`, and `card_not_nows`? Are all indexes working for our complex query?

2.  **Due Cards**: Many cards are due, and this causes the O(N\^2) problem, or `find_each` runs many batches. If it's the `find_each` execution, even with 100,000 cards, it would be 30s.

3.  **ActiveRecord Batches & Queries**: I need to check the exact queries generated by `find_each` to see if there is something problematic with the execution of the `where` clause on the query.

4.  **SQLite Configuration**: Does WAL mode or concurrent writers, or the database's cache settings play a role? Is there a disk I/O bottleneck? This seems unlikely given the focused nature of the issue.

I keep coming back to this: In our test DB, with only a few sample records, the query is fast. The problem emerges when the `cards` table grows.

My next steps will be to generate a test SQLite database with a realistic number of records and run an `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` on our `SELECT` statement with:

*   100k cards
*   90k closures
*   5k card\_not\_nows
*   500 boards
*   100 accounts

I'll see what the query plan looks like and determine if this helps us identify the source of the problem.

Wait, back up...why did my benchmark only take a fraction of a second? The data I used in the benchmark was *highly* specific: 100,000 cards all on a single board, with identical `last_active_at`, and no other related data. No complex relationships. No `ANALYZE`. Let me think this through. What if the real problem is this: the query is doing a full table scan? The `due_to_be_postponed` scope can't use an index on `last_active_at` across all accounts. class Filter < ApplicationRecord
  include Fields, Params, Resources, Summarized

  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }
  belongs_to :account, default: -> { creator.account }

  class << self
    def from_params(params)
      find_by_params(params) || build(params)
    end

    def remember(attrs)
      create!(attrs)
    rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique
      find_by_params(attrs).tap(&:touch)
    end
  end

  def cards
    @cards ||= begin
      result = creator.accessible_cards.preloaded.published
      result = result.indexed_by(indexed_by)
      result = result.sorted_by(sorted_by)
      result = result.where(id: card_ids) if card_ids.present?
      result = result.where.missing(:not_now) unless include_not_now_cards?
      result = result.open unless include_closed_cards?
      result = result.unassigned if assignment_status.unassigned?
      result = result.assigned_to(assignees.ids) if assignees.present?
      result = result.where(creator_id: creators.ids) if creators.present?
      result = result.where(board: boards.ids) if boards.present?
      result = result.tagged_with(tags.ids) if tags.present?
      result = result.where(cards: { created_at: creation_window }) if creation_window
      result = result.closed_at_window(closure_window) if closure_window
      result = result.closed_by(closers) if closers.present?
      result = terms.reduce(result) do |result, term|
        result.mentioning(term, user: creator)
      end
      result = result.where(column_id: column_ids) if column_ids.present?

      result.distinct
    end
  end

  def empty?
    self.class.normalize_params(as_params).blank?
  end

  def single_board
    boards.first if boards.one?
  end

  def single_workflow
    boards.first.workflow if boards.pluck(:workflow_id).uniq.one?
  end

  def cacheable?
    boards.exists?
  end

  def cache_key
    ActiveSupport::Cache.expand_cache_key params_digest, "filter"
  end

  def only_closed?
    indexed_by.closed? || closure_window || closers.present?
  end

  private
    def include_closed_cards?
      only_closed? || card_ids.present?
    end

    def include_not_now_cards?
      indexed_by.not_now? || card_ids.present?
    end
end

**Analyzing a Performance Bottleneck: Card.due_to_be_postponed**

Okay, hold on a second! I need to really dig into why `Card.due_to_be_postponed` is grinding to a halt on a larger dataset, specifically around 100,000 cards in SQLite. My initial thought process is to trace through the code, focusing on the `Card::Entropic` module and those `due_to_be_postponed` and `auto_postpone_all_due` scopes. Let's start by scrutinizing the SQL generated by that scope.

I'm seeing a complex `JOIN` operation across several tables: `cards`, `boards`, `accounts`, `entropies`, and `account_entropies`. The core of the issue looks to be this `WHERE` clause: `last_active_at <= datetime(?, '-' || COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period) || ' seconds')`. The key here is the `last_active_at` comparison. The right-hand side is derived from a `COALESCE` on `entropies.auto_postpone_period` and `account_entropies.auto_postpone_period`. This makes the comparison, and thus the entire `WHERE` clause, non-SARGable.

Wait, it just struck me: **the critical problem is the index usage, or rather, the lack thereof**. I can't use an index directly on `last_active_at` because the right-hand side of the comparison is dynamically calculated via a function (`COALESCE`), and therefore, it can't leverage an index efficiently. Furthermore, there isn't an index on `last_active_at` specifically! The existing index is on `account_id`, `last_active_at`, and `status`. I'm concerned about the index's efficiency, even in cases where the `account_id` is fixed, as the `last_active_at` is *before* `status` in the index's definition.

Furthermore, it becomes clear that this query does *not* filter by `account_id` at all, which is alarming. Instead, it relies on a join through `boards`. `find_each` then adds an `ORDER BY "cards"."id" ASC LIMIT 1000`, which is adding insult to injury. With 100,000+ cards, SQLite has to scan the `sqlite_autoindex_cards_1`, which is the primary key index.

I'm now putting it together: the combination of a non-SARGable comparison, a missing direct index on the relevant column (`last_active_at`), and the `find_each` iterator with its `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` is the perfect storm for a performance disaster. It's essentially a full table scan, fetching every single card row.

Now, I need to consider edge cases and configurations, particularly, what if `SolidQueue` or other background processing systems are interfering, or if the database settings (`PRAGMA`) are impacting the query plan? Could this be impacted by different data distributions in the joined tables? It seems someone saw the same problem I am seeing now: the hourly entropy sweep failing to complete. This is supported by the APM data and AppSignal logs. I think it is time to do some quick tests to confirm my hypothesis.

**Deep Dive into Card Postponement Performance**

Okay, let's break this down. We need to optimize `Card.due_to_be_postponed` and `Card.auto_postpone_all_due`. The current implementation is clearly suffering performance issues, specifically full table scans, and we need to understand WHY.

First, I see the query itself:

scope :due_to_be_postponed, -> do
  active
    .joins(board: :account)
    .left_outer_joins(board: :entropy)
    .joins("LEFT OUTER JOIN entropies AS account_entropies ON account_entropies.account_id = accounts.id AND account_entropies.container_type = 'Account' AND account_entropies.container_id = accounts.id")
    .where("last_active_at <= #{connection.date_subtract('?', 'COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period)')}", Time.now)
end

and the auto-postponing method:

class_methods do
  def auto_postpone_all_due
    due_to_be_postponed.find_each do |card|
      card.auto_postpone(user: card.account.system_user)
    end

Right away, I see the potential for a bottleneck. Here's what's jumping out at me:

1.  **The Full Table Scan:** The `cards` table is being scanned entirely on every execution. The existing indexes, especially `index_cards_on_account_id_and_last_active_at_and_status`, are not being utilized effectively. `find_each` is ordered by `id`, but the query condition involves a comparison with `last_active_at`. We have a join to boards, accounts, entropies. This means that we're doing a lot of lookups for every single card. Ninety-nine percent of them will be filtered out.

2.  **Index Inefficiency:** The core of the problem is the `WHERE` clause: `last_active_at <= COALESCE(...)`. The `COALESCE` is the killer. Since the comparison relies on a value computed from joined tables, the database cannot use a range scan on `last_active_at`. The database has to evaluate the `COALESCE` for *every* row, making any index on `last_active_at` irrelevant.

3.  **Lack of Account-Specific Filtering:** The fact that `due_to_be_postponed` *doesn't* constrain `cards.account_id` up front also hurts index usage. We're looking across *all* accounts. While `account_id` is an index, we cannot leverage the account ID's index.

4.  **`find_each`:**  The current use of `find_each` within `auto_postpone_all_due` does not batch loads and is likely making multiple database calls.

But, before we make any radical changes, we need to think about a few subtleties.

*   **Subtlety 1: The Scope:** `due_to_be_postponed` isn't just used internally. It's a public scope. It needs to keep its semantics. *Any* external code could be calling it directly, and the results it returns need to be correct.

*   **Subtlety 2: The Exact Semantics of `due_to_be_postponed`:**  We need to nail down the precise meaning of this scope:
    *   What does `active` really mean? We have `open`, `published`, and `not_now`.
    *   How does the `board` and `account` join work?  The `left_outer_joins` on `entropy` are critical. If an account or board doesn't have an `entropy` record, the `COALESCE` will evaluate to `NULL`, and that's going to affect the results.
    *   The values of `Entropy::AUTO_POSTPONE_PERIODS_IN_SECONDS` are important. It is possible that the entropy values are not constant (e.g. 3 days), so the code cannot be hard-coded around this. The code will need to accommodate variable postpone periods.

We need to consider these factors when designing an optimized solution.

messages.content: Let's compare indexes in `db/schema.rb` vs `db/schema_sqlite.rb` to see if there are any discrepancies.
messages.thinking:
**Analyzing the Performance Bottleneck**

Okay, here's what I'm thinking, trying to get to the bottom of this performance issue. I see a *massive* slowdown in `Card.due_to_be_postponed`, jumping from a few seconds in a controlled test environment to nearly an hour in a real-world scenario. That's a huge red flag!

First, the query itself. I'm focusing on the joins, the `WHERE` clause, and the index usage (or lack thereof). My initial thought is that the *missing* index on `cards` is the main culprit. Specifically, there's no index covering `(status, last_active_at)` or even `(board_id, status, last_active_at)`. With a large dataset, this lack of indexing will lead to a full table scan, and that is very slow.

However, SQLite's behavior is giving me pause. Even *with* an index on `(status, last_active_at)`, the SQLite query optimizer may choose to scan the whole table if `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` is present, or the RHS of `last_active_at` depends on the joined tables (as it does). It really depends on what is happening in the current SQL.

Now, consider the real-world scenario. Most cards will be closed or postponed, and their `last_active_at` will be old. That means *even* with an index, the query will still have to check a vast majority of the cards against the `closures` and `card_not_nows` tables, which is very inefficient. I'm thinking that's the real problem, especially if the code doesn't update `last_active_at` when a card is closed or postponed. I have to check the code in `app/models/card/closeable.rb`, `app/models/card/postponable.rb`, and `app/models/card/eventable.rb`.

Then there is the APM sample. The 58-minute duration is completely out of proportion with the 0.183 second in the test, which just doesn't make sense. I'm thinking about *every* factor that could cause such an extreme slowdown: a different `SQLite` configuration, different indexes on tables, different states in the tables, and the `ANALYZE` command. The APM sample, it says the query is spending most of the time in `sql.active_record`, which gives an important clue.

I am now looking for *any* case where `SQLite` scans the `cards` table AND does a full table scan on any of the joined tables. I have to double-check the indexes in `db/schema_sqlite.rb` and `db/migrate/`! Finally, I have to compare `db/schema_sqlite.rb` and `db/schema.rb`, looking for differences that could explain this issue.

arguments.command: diff -u <(grep "create_table\|t\.index" db/schema.rb | sed 's/, charset:.*force:/, force:/') <(grep "create_table\|t\.index" db/schema_sqlite.rb) || true

class Account::DataTransfer::EntropyRecordSet < Account::DataTransfer::RecordSet
  def initialize(account)
    super(account: account, model: Entropy)
  end

  private
    def import_batch(files)
      batch_data = files.map do |file|
        data = load(file)
        data.slice(*attributes).merge("account_id" => account.id)

      end

**Deep Dive into Optimizing Card Postponement Logic**

Okay, so I'm looking at this code, and it's screaming for optimization. I see `cache_size: 2000`, which is fine, but the real bottleneck is the *algorithm* itself. We're doing a full table scan on ALL cards (100,000+ cards, joining six tables per card!) every time we check for postponement. That's inefficient, plain and simple. We need to identify a cleaner, faster, and more idiomatic solution.

So, let's break this down like a senior Rails/database engineer would.  We need to ask: Can we avoid scanning closed and postponed cards, or recent cards, or both?  Let's do a *deep dive* analysis.

Here's the problem: A card is `due_to_be_postponed` if it meets several criteria: it needs to be `published`, open (no entry in `closures`), not postponed (no entry in `card_not_nows`), and it must have been inactive for longer than a configurable period defined by `board.entropy` or `account.entropy`.

Now, if we consider that we have a massive database of 100,000+ cards, the breakdown looks something like this: 85% are closed, 10% are postponed, and only 5% are active. Out of that 5%, a tiny fraction (maybe only 0.01% - 100 cards) are actually eligible for postponement.

So, how do we get from 100,000 cards down to those ~100?

**Method 1: Index on `[:status, :last_active_at]`**

My first instinct is to add an index.  But, wait, here's the problem. Even with an index on `[:status, :last_active_at]` (or even `[:board_id, :status, :last_active_at]`), if we filter on cards that have `status = 'published'` and  `last_active_at <= 30.days.ago`, and 95,000 cards have `last_active_at <= 30.days.ago`, we *still* have to scan a huge chunk of our table! We’re *still* matching 95,000 rows, and performing 190,000 lookups (closures and card_not_nows).  As the data grows, we’re still doing an O(total historical cards) scan of the database, which is going to be slow.

**Method 2: How Do We Skip ALL That Noise?**

Okay, we need to be smarter. We *need* to skip those closed and postponed cards *entirely* and also those recently active cards. Why are we even checking against `closures` and `card_not_nows` for all these records in the first place? We need to analyze this further.

**Way 2A: Partial Indexes?**

Can we use a partial index?  But SQLite's partial indexes can't reference those other tables (`closures`, `card_not_nows`). MySQL doesn't even support partial indexes. We'd need something on the `cards` table itself to make this work.  A partial index is out.

**Way 2B: Let's Re-Think the Data Model**

So, we need to think deeper. What if the `cards` table *itself* had a way to indicate that a card is _not_ relevant.  Could we use a column on `cards`? Maybe we could work with `NOT IN`, `EXISTS`?  But even `NOT EXISTS` would require probing `closures` and `card_not_nows` for every `(status = 'published' AND last_active_at <= cutoff)` row. We need to *avoid* that.

What about driving our lookup from the **active** cards versus using `last_active_at` as the driver? We need an *active cards* index. But there isn't one unless we track that directly, or have a separate table.

class NotificationsDataMigration < ActiveRecord::Migration[8.2]
  BATCH_SIZE = 10_000

  class Notification < ActiveRecord::Base
    self.table_name = "notifications"
  end

  def change
    reversible do |dir|
      dir.up do
        populate_card_id
        collapse_duplicates
      end
    end

    change_column_null :notifications, :card_id, false
    add_index :notifications, [ :user_id, :card_id ], unique: true
  end

  private
    def populate_card_id
      execute(<<~SQL)
        UPDATE notifications
        SET card_id = (
          SELECT CASE events.eventable_type
            WHEN 'Card' THEN events.eventable_id
            WHEN 'Comment' THEN (SELECT comments.card_id FROM comments WHERE comments.id = events.eventable_id)
          END
          FROM events
          WHERE events.id = notifications.source_id
        )
        WHERE notifications.card_id IS NULL
          AND notifications.source_type = 'Event'
      SQL

      execute(<<~SQL)
        UPDATE notifications
        SET card_id = (
          SELECT CASE mentions.source_type
            WHEN 'Card' THEN mentions.source_id
            WHEN 'Comment' THEN (SELECT comments.card_id FROM comments WHERE comments.id = mentions.source_id)
          END
          FROM mentions
          WHERE mentions.id = notifications.source_id
        )
        WHERE notifications.card_id IS NULL
          AND notifications.source_type = 'Mention'
      SQL
    end

    def collapse_duplicates
      loop do
        duplicates = Notification.find_by_sql(<<~SQL)
          SELECT user_id, card_id,
                 MAX(id) AS keep_id,
                 COUNT(*) AS total,
                 SUM(CASE WHEN read_at IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS unread_total
          FROM notifications
          WHERE card_id IS NOT NULL
          GROUP BY user_id, card_id
          HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
          LIMIT #{BATCH_SIZE}
        SQL

        break if duplicates.empty?

        duplicates.each do |row|
          Notification.where(user_id: row.user_id, card_id: row.card_id)
            .where.not(id: row.keep_id)
            .delete_all

          Notification.where(id: row.keep_id)
            .update_all(unread_count: row.unread_total.to_i)
        end
      end

      # Set unread_count for remaining non-collapsed notifications
      execute(<<~SQL)
        UPDATE notifications
        SET unread_count = CASE WHEN read_at IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
        WHERE unread_count = 0 AND card_id IS NOT NULL
      SQL
    end
end
"

Right, okay, I've got it! That benchmark really highlighted a critical difference. In the test database, `/tmp/bench.sqlite3`, only 2,600 cards matched the `last_active_at <= cutoff` criteria. But, in a *real* production environment, after months or years of operation, all 95,000 closed and postponed cards *also* satisfy that same condition! Bingo!

We need to simulate that realistic data distribution in `/tmp/bench.sqlite3`. Let's tweak the `last_active_at` values. For the 80,000 closed cards, let's set `last_active_at = 60.days.ago`, and for the 15,000 postponed ones, the same. And for those 5,000 active cards, how about `1.day.ago` (with 10 due)?

Now, let's compare some approaches:
1.  The original query (`due_to_be_postponed.find_each`).
2.  The index on `[:status, :last_active_at]` *with* a constant cutoff (which, crucially, still touches all those 95,000 closed/postponed cards!).
3.  The most important part... can we drive the query from the active cards rather than closed/postponed? Essentially, how can we *avoid* touching those 95,000 cards altogether?!

Time to run that benchmark with this new, realistic data set and see what we can learn!

ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: "/tmp/bench.sqlite3")

recent = 1.day.ago.utc.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%6N")
conn.execute("UPDATE cards SET last_active_at = \"#{old}\" WHERE id IN (SELECT card_id FROM closures) OR id IN (SELECT card_id FROM card_not_nows)")

# Make 10 active cards due
Card.active.limit(10).update_all(last_active_at: 60.days.ago)
conn.execute("ANALYZE")

Okay, here's my take on those thoughts, tailored for an expert audience:

**SQL String Literal Conundrum**

Right, a minor but potentially irritating detail just popped into my head. I was just thinking about the best practice for string literals in SQLite. Specifically, I need to remind myself, and likely future collaborators, that using single quotes is the standard and preferred method for delineating string literals in SQLite SQL statements. Double quotes, although sometimes *technically* permissible depending on the context, can lead to ambiguity and potential parsing issues, especially when dealing with nested quotes or identifiers. It’s always best to be consistent and avoid that potential headache. Single quotes it is – keeps things clean and predictable.

        "X-Webhook-Timestamp" => event.created_at.utc.iso8601
      }
    end

    def signature
      OpenSSL::HMAC.hexdigest("SHA256", webhook.signing_secret, payload)
    end

    def content_type
      if webhook.for_campfire?
        "text/html"
      elsif webhook.for_basecamp?
        "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"
      else
        "application/json"
      end
    end

    def payload
      @payload ||= if webhook.for_basecamp?
        { content: render_payload(formats: :html) }.to_query
      elsif webhook.for_campfire?
        render_payload(formats: :html)
      elsif webhook.for_slack?
        slack_payload
      else
        render_payload(formats: :json)
      end
    end

    def render_payload(**options)
      webhook.renderer.render(layout: false, template: "webhooks/event", assigns: { event: event }, **options).strip

      document = Nokogiri::HTML5(html)

      document.css("a").each do |a|
        a.replace("<#{a["href"].strip}|#{a.text}>") if a["href"].present?
      end

      document.css("b").each do |b|
        b.replace("*#{b.text}*")
      end

      document.css("i").each do |i|
        i.replace("_#{i.text}_")
      end

      document.text
    end

    def slack_payload
      text = event.description_for(nil).to_plain_text
      url = polymorphic_url(event.eventable, base_url_options.merge(script_name: account.slug))

      { text: "#{text} <#{url}|Open in Fizzy>" }.to_json
    end

    def base_url_options
      Rails.application.routes.default_url_options.presence ||
        Rails.application.config.action_mailer.default_url_options
    end

Alright, let's break this down. My initial instinct was to focus on index optimization and query rewriting, tweaking `Card::Entropic` and the database schemas (`db/schema_sqlite.rb`, `db/schema.rb`). Lack of indexes on `[:status, :last_active_at]`, the per-row joined expression, and the `find_each`'s inherent `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` were the obvious culprits. And the active join with `closures` and `card_not_nows` - meaning a lot of rows being scanned are inactive.

2.  My first strategy: Query + index. I figured, add an index, rewrite the queries to use it, and we should be golden. I test it, and its a slight improvement... but only 22%!

But then, that number hit me like a ton of bricks: **22% faster**, and 95,000 out of 100,000 cards were old and closed/postponed. It barely made a dent. Even a 50% reduction in time wouldn't solve a 58-minute job. The conclusion hit me that even with indexes and optimized queries, the massive number of irrelevant rows matching the initial `WHERE` clause was the true bottleneck.

And that's when the big picture became crystal clear. My gut reaction was to look at SQLite and the `cards` table. In a real-world scenario with 100,000+ cards, the sheer size of the database, the interleaved data, and the random access patterns caused by the `sqlite_autoindex_cards_1` index would be KILLING performance, resulting in repeated disk seeks and page faults. No matter how clever the query, it was going to be slow.

My current focus: it's not the queries, but the *data*. The fix must *avoid* scanning the majority of the rows. This translates to avoiding scanning these cards:
*   Drafted cards (`status = 'drafted'`)
*   Closed cards (cards with a `Closure`)
*   Postponed cards (cards with a `Card::NotNow`)
*   Recently active cards (`last_active_at > cutoff`)

The goal is to isolate the *actual* work to only the eligible cards.

Cause 1 is that the current approach with `COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period)` and the missing index causes a full table scan and multiple index lookups for every card. Cause 2 adds to this because even with a cutoff and index, we're still unnecessarily scanning a vast majority of closed and postponed cards.

My immediate focus is finding a way to solve BOTH of these problems. I'm trying to figure out how to do it efficiently, safely, and without introducing any regressions. The `Account::DataTransfer` export/import functionality and fixtures are a critical consideration.

Can we avoid adding new columns to the `cards` table, since adding a column could break `Account::DataTransfer`? My initial thought is to try a covering index on `cards`, like `[:status, :last_active_at, :board_id, :id]`. If the query just selects `cards.id`, then SQLite should be able to check the status, last active time, and existence of related records in `closures` and `card_not_nows` using only the index. But even then, there will be a significant number of index lookups, especially as the database grows. So even if the covering index helps, it's not a complete solution. cutoff = 30.days.ago.utc.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%6N")

# Q1: Join closures & not_nows first using covering index, then filter boards/entropies
q1 = <<~SQL
  SELECT cards.id
  FROM cards
  LEFT OUTER JOIN closures ON closures.card_id = cards.id
  LEFT OUTER JOIN card_not_nows AS not_now ON not_now.card_id = cards.id
  INNER JOIN boards ON boards.id = cards.board_id
  INNER JOIN accounts ON accounts.id = boards.account_id
  LEFT OUTER JOIN entropies ON entropies.container_type = '\''Board'\'' AND entropies.container_id = boards.id
  LEFT OUTER JOIN entropies AS account_entropies ON account_entropies.account_id = accounts.id AND account_entropies.container_type = '\''Account'\'' AND account_entropies.container_id = accounts.id
  WHERE cards.status = '\''published'\''
    AND cards.last_active_at <= '\''#{cutoff}'\''
    AND closures.id IS NULL
    AND not_now.id IS NULL
    AND cards.last_active_at <= datetime('\''#{Time.now.utc.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%6N")}'\'', '\''-'\'' || COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period) || '\'' seconds'\'')
SQL

# Q2: Subquery / CTE filtering active + cutoff first, then joining boards/entropies
q2 = <<~SQL
  SELECT c.id
  FROM (
    SELECT cards.id, cards.board_id, cards.last_active_at
    FROM cards
    WHERE cards.status = '\''published'\''
      AND cards.last_active_at <= '\''#{cutoff}'\''
      AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM closures WHERE closures.card_id = cards.id)
      AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM card_not_nows WHERE card_not_nows.card_id = cards.id)
  ) AS c
  INNER JOIN boards ON boards.id = c.board_id
  INNER JOIN accounts ON accounts.id = boards.account_id
  LEFT OUTER JOIN entropies ON entropies.container_type = '\''Board'\'' AND entropies.container_id = boards.id
  LEFT OUTER JOIN entropies AS account_entropies ON account_entropies.account_id = accounts.id AND account_entropies.container_type = '\''Account'\'' AND account_entropies.container_id = accounts.id
  WHERE c.last_active_at <= datetime('\''#{Time.now.utc.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%6N")}'\'', '\''-'\'' || COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period) || '\'' seconds'\'')
SQL

# Q3: NOT IN (closures)
q3 = <<~SQL
  SELECT cards.id
  FROM cards
  WHERE cards.status = '\''published'\''
    AND cards.last_active_at <= '\''#{cutoff}'\''
    AND cards.id NOT IN (SELECT card_id FROM closures)
    AND cards.id NOT IN (SELECT card_id FROM card_not_nows)
SQL

# Q4: What if we query ALL active cards (without last_active_at <= cutoff) vs with cutoff?
q4 = <<~SQL
  SELECT cards.id
  FROM cards
  WHERE cards.status = '\''published'\''
    AND cards.id NOT IN (SELECT card_id FROM closures)
    AND cards.id NOT IN (SELECT card_id FROM card_not_nows)
    AND cards.last_active_at <= '\''#{cutoff}'\''
SQL

What if we use the *board's* auto_postpone_period to construct the `WHERE` clauses? Grouping by period and querying only the relevant boards is the ticket. This means that a 365-day board never sees cards due in 3 days.

And the best way to do that is to have a covering index on `board_id, status, last_active_at, id` and then chunk board ids and scan only the relevant cards that belong to those boards!

Now, the `due_to_be_postponed` scope itself is the target, and we can make this scope faster. The current implementation fetches all the data, and then it is slower than the optimized way. We can optimize it by getting the results of the scope and sending it off to `find_each`. We can select `:id` with covering index, and send the results to `find_each` in batches.

Finally, regarding `find_each`, fetching IDs in one query with the index (then slicing them), and then using `.includes` to fetch everything in batches is a huge win. The `find_each` loop can process in batches.

In summary, the key improvements are:
1.  Using `COVERING INDEX` on the `cards` table.
2.  Grouping by `board_id` and querying boards by `period`.
3.  Optimizing `due_to_be_postponed` to pluck the `:id` with the covering index, and then using `.includes` on batches of those cards.

My immediate concern is around the query performance of `q2` when dealing with a large number of cards. I want to understand what's happening at scale—will this be fast regardless of the total card count? Why is the query scanning so many entries when we have covering indexes?

The problem is that even with our indexes, the query is still touching a significant number of records in `tmp_idx_cards_covering` due to the large volume of closed/postponed cards that match the `status = 'published'` and `last_active_at <= cutoff` criteria. Though we use a covering index, we are still doing more work than required. This takes ~30 MB sequentially and is slower with more cards. The subsequent index probes on `index_closures_on_card_id` and `index_card_not_nows_on_card_id` aren't *that* bad. The disk I/O cost isn't bad on its own. It's the overall work that I want to remove if possible.

My goal is to eliminate this scan entirely for closed/postponed cards to get as close to O(1) as possible, regardless of the size of the total dataset.

The natural idea is to add a column (e.g., `active` or `state`) to the `cards` table to indicate whether a card is active. However, I know the code pretty well; based on experience, that seems problematic for a few reasons. Adding a column to `cards` would introduce potential issues with our existing data transfer and import mechanisms. Tests rely on directly inserting/deleting `closures` and `card_not_nows` using raw SQL, which could leave the `cards` table out of sync.

So, let's explore an alternative, keeping in mind existing constraints.

I recall previous benchmarking where `NOT IN` performed better than `NOT EXISTS`. I want to investigate this. The `NOT IN` construct might be faster because SQLite can build a temporary index/hash internally (or probe the existing index directly). This leads to better performance than `NOT EXISTS`, which relies on correlated subqueries. In MySQL, the performance behavior is completely different; `NOT EXISTS` is *always* an antijoin in MySQL 8 and uses covering indexes in both SQLite and MySQL. And the difference between `q2` and `q3` is < 0.1s! Practically, these seem equivalent.

RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails runner '
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: "/tmp/bench.sqlite3")
conn = ActiveRecord::Base.connection
now = Time.now

# 1. Covering index (status, last_active_at, board_id, id) + min_period + NOT EXISTS
min_period = Entropy.minimum(:auto_postpone_period)
t1 = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
ids_min = Card
  .published
  .where(last_active_at: ..(now - min_period))
  .where("NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM closures WHERE closures.card_id = cards.id)")
  .where("NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM card_not_nows WHERE card_not_nows.card_id = cards.id)")
  .joins(board: :account)
  .left_outer_joins(board: :entropy)
  .joins("LEFT OUTER JOIN entropies AS account_entropies ON account_entropies.account_id = accounts.id AND account_entropies.container_type = '\''Account'\'' AND account_entropies.container_id = accounts.id")
  .where("cards.last_active_at <= #{conn.date_subtract("?", "COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period)")}", now)
  .pluck(:id)
t_min = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) - t1

# 2. Grouped by period using (board_id, status, last_active_at, id) + NOT EXISTS
t1 = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
board_entropies = Entropy.where(container_type: "Board").pluck(:container_id, :auto_postpone_period).to_h
account_entropies = Entropy.where(container_type: "Account").pluck(:container_id, :auto_postpone_period).to_h

by_period = Hash.new { |h, k| h[k] = [] }
Board.pluck(:id, :account_id).each do |bid, aid|
  period = board_entropies[bid] || account_entropies[aid]
  by_period[period] << bid if period
end

ids_board = []
by_period.each do |period, bids|
  cutoff = now - period
  bids.each_slice(500) do |batch_bids|
    ids_board.concat(
      Card.published

        .where("NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM closures WHERE closures.card_id = cards.id)")
        .where("NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM card_not_nows WHERE card_not_nows.card_id = cards.id)")
        .pluck(:id)
    )
  end
end
t_board = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) - t1

puts "2) grouped by period + NOT EXISTS (2051 boards, 100k cards): #{t_board.round(4)}s, count=#{ids_board.size}"

messages.thinking:
**Incredible Database Optimization with SQLite!**

Okay, here's what's going through my mind: I'm seeing some absolutely brilliant behavior from SQLite. Specifically, I'm blown away by how it utilizes `DeferredSeek` (instruction 15) and covering indexes to minimize I/O, especially when dealing with potentially large datasets. The way it avoids touching the `cards` table at all for cards that are closed, postponed, or not due is genius, as long as `(status, last_active_at, board_id, id)` are present in the covering index. It's essentially filtering based on the index data alone *before* ever hitting the main table. The `cards` table is only read when we actually output a due card!

I'm making a mental note to double-check why the covering index included the specific columns (`status`, `last_active_at`, `board_id`, `id`) and it all seems to tie together. The predicate columns in the WHERE clause, along with the columns in the covering index, allow it to filter effectively.

Now, I'm starting to think critically. What if we use `find_each` to iterate over those due cards? Let's check the query plan with `EXPLAIN` to make sure we're still getting the benefits of that covering index. I wonder if SQLite would pick a different index if the `tmp_idx_cards_status_last_active` index was available. What if we only create `[:status, :last_active_at, :board_id, :id]`? If the `tmp_idx_cards_status_last_active` doesn't exist, SQLite would always choose `[:status, :last_active_at, :board_id, :id]` which should be the optimal index.

I'm also considering the mixed-period scenario, with boards having vastly different auto-postpone periods. We need to make sure the queries still perform well in this case. Would grouping by period offer any advantage? Can `Card.due_to_be_postponed` handle both scenarios gracefully? The scope definition (`Option A`) has me wondering if it can handle the scenarios and whether the `postponing_soon` scope is optimized. It is worth evaluating whether the scopes are optimized based on the bounds.

I'm now zeroing in on the `auto_postpone_all_due` method. The use of `find_each` here raises a red flag. I'm seeing potential for N+1 query problems due to the `card.account.system_user` call. Caching the `system_user` or preloading the `account` would reduce the number of queries and make the process more efficient. Also, the choice of `find_each`, `pluck(:id)`, or grouping by period impacts performance. I need to benchmark these approaches.

Finally, I'm thinking about the scale. What if the `cards` table grows to 500,000 or even a million rows? We need to ensure these optimizations hold up. I must benchmark `Option A` on 100,000 cards (with the covering index only) and test `find_each`, `pluck(:id)`, `count`, and `auto_postpone_all_due`. That's how we'll confirm we've created something truly efficient.

RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails runner '
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: "/tmp/bench.sqlite3")
conn = ActiveRecord::Base.connection
conn.execute("DROP INDEX IF EXISTS tmp_idx_cards_status_last_active")
conn.execute("DROP INDEX IF EXISTS tmp_idx_cards_board_covering")
conn.execute("ANALYZE")

now = Time.now
min_period = Entropy.minimum(:auto_postpone_period)
rel = Card
  .published
  .where(last_active_at: ..(now - min_period))
  .where("NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM closures WHERE closures.card_id = cards.id)")
  .where("NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM card_not_nows WHERE card_not_nows.card_id = cards.id)")
  .joins(board: :account)
  .left_outer_joins(board: :entropy)
  .joins("LEFT OUTER JOIN entropies AS account_entropies ON account_entropies.account_id = accounts.id AND account_entropies.container_type = '\''Account'\'' AND account_entropies.container_id = accounts.id")
  .where("cards.last_active_at <= #{conn.date_subtract("?", "COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period)")}", now)

puts "=== find_each EQP ==="
conn.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN #{rel.order(:id).limit(1000).to_sql}").each { |r| p r }
t1 = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
c = 0; rel.find_each { c += 1 }
puts "find_each time: #{(Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) - t1).round(4)}s, count=#{c}"

puts "=== pluck(:id) EQP ==="
conn.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN #{rel.select(:id).to_sql}").each { |r| p r }
t1 = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
ids = rel.pluck(:id)
puts "pluck(:id) time: #{(Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) - t1).round(4)}s, count=#{ids.size}"
'

messages.thinking:
**Analyzing and Optimizing Card Postponement Logic**

Okay, here's the breakdown of my thought process as I've been dissecting this card postponement feature. I need to make sure this is as efficient as humanly possible, especially with larger datasets and potentially slow disks.

First off, I need to make sure `find_each` is not inefficient. If 10,000 cards are due, and `find_each` runs 10 batches, each batch re-scans the table when there is a condition such as `cards.id > ?`. This means, with the current index, the database would have to repeatedly scan the entire set of candidates and sort them in a temporary B-tree, causing slow queries. `pluck(:id)` in this scenario appears to be dramatically superior. This will run faster, as it uses the existing `(status, last_active_at, board_id, id)` index for a single, initial query and avoids repeated full scans.

Now, let's consider the broader picture, and also test:
1) If 10,000 cards are due and `find_each` runs 10 batches:
   Notice `find_each` adds `cards.id > ?` on batches 2..10!
   With `tmp_idx_cards_covering (status, last_active_at, board_id, id)`:
   SQLite CANNOT use `cards.id > ?` in the index `(status, last_active_at, board_id, id)`!
   So EVERY ONE of the 10 batches re-scans from the beginning of `(status = 'published', last_active_at <= min_cutoff)`, checks all 95k closures, sorts all remaining due cards in `TEMP B-TREE`, and takes the first 1000!
   If 50,000 cards are due, `find_each` runs **50 times** (`50 * 0.14s = 7s`, or on slow disk 50x worse)!
   WHEREAS `due_to_be_postponed.pluck(:id)` runs **ONCE** (`0.07s`), then slices by 1000 (`where(id: batch_ids)`) — **50x fewer scans**!

2) `due_to_be_postponed` does NOT rescan and sort a huge intermediate result (just the covering index is scanned).

3) I need to make sure the indices are correctly leveraged. A proper covering index, especially in SQLite, is KEY for performance. I need to confirm the presence of `:id` in the index `[:status, :last_active_at, :board_id, :id]`. In SQLite, unlike InnoDB's implicit clustered index on `id`, `id` is required in the index for effective covering index operations, since otherwise it reads the `rowid` from the main table.

Now, let's verify that with the `auto_postpone_all_due` function, we're not running into issues.

-   If `Entropy.minimum(:auto_postpone_period)` returns `nil` (no entropy records), the due date logic will be correctly handled, which means no cards are affected. The same applies to association scopes (`board.cards.due_to_be_postponed` returns an empty relation if there is no period specified).
-   If `Entropy` is updated, the dynamic evaluation of `Entropy.minimum(:auto_postpone_period)` in the lambda ensures the logic is consistent, but it is important to check if it has a noticeable impact on SQL performance and add caching, as it runs an SQL query every time.
-   SQLite's `datetime(...)` function truncates subseconds, which would cause an inaccurate comparison if we use subseconds from `Time.now` in a comparison. I need to make sure there are no issues.
-   The use of `NOT EXISTS` seems ideal. It's self-contained and avoids polluting the `LEFT OUTER JOIN` table aliases, which is safe.
-   Lastly, `find_each` on very large result sets is a no-go. The database will re-scan and resort for each batch.

I need to test and be sure the queries run as efficiently as possible, especially with edge cases.

messages.thinking:
**Optimizing Card Due Date Postponement Logic**

Okay, so I'm looking at this `Account#system_user` call and thinking about how to eliminate potential N+1 query issues. The current `users.find_by!(role: :system)` is a red flag.  The naive `preload(account: :users)` isn't sufficient to prevent the lookup, so a memoized lookup of the `system_user` based on `account_id` seems like a much better approach. Either a simple memoized lookup like `system_users[card.account_id] ||= card.account.system_user` or preloading with something like `User.where(account_id: ..., role: :system).index_by(&:account_id)` will work. This avoids all those extra queries!

The `due_to_be_postponed.pluck(:id)` call is interesting. If that list is empty, which I expect is true 99% of the time, then it's fantastic because it adds *zero* overhead! If it *does* contain card IDs, then slicing it into batches of 1000 using `batch_ids`, loading the cards, and then caching the `system_users` by `account_id` is an efficient way to handle it. We can still fall back to `card.account.system_user` to maintain the `RecordNotFound` behavior in case some account is missing a system user.

But wait a minute, let's go back and reconsider our approach to `due_to_be_postponed.pluck(:id)` in light of the `Board`-grouped query and `find_each` approaches.

Remember we were thinking about a scenario where one board has a very short `auto_postpone_period` (like 3 days) and another board has a much longer period (365 days) with tons of active cards?

Let's evaluate *both* of those options:

*   **Option 1 (`min_period` in `due_to_be_postponed`)**: A single query like `published.where(last_active_at: ..(now - min_period)).where("NOT EXISTS ...").joins(...)` is very tempting. It works on any relation (`Card.due_to_be_postponed`, `board.cards.due_to_be_postponed`, `account.cards.due_to_be_postponed`). And the use of a covering index `[:status, :last_active_at, :board_id, :id]` is a bonus. If most boards have a `30.days` period, or most cards are closed or postponed, this option is fast and efficient.  It might take ~0.07s on 100,000 cards. Or is it better to just have the `min_period`? Consider a system with 2000 boards, each with distinct postpone periods. Using `where(last_active_at: ..(now - min_period))` is ideal. It translates to a single SQL query, regardless of the board count. *   **Scenario 2:** 100,000 cards with *most* of them being active on a single board with a *long* period, and one board with a short period.

module Card::Entropic
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    scope :due_to_be_postponed, -> do
      now = Time.now

      if min_period = Entropy.minimum(:auto_postpone_period)
        published
          .where(last_active_at: ..(now - min_period))
          .where("NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM closures WHERE closures.card_id = cards.id)")
          .where("NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM card_not_nows WHERE card_not_nows.card_id = cards.id)")
          .joins(board: :account)
          .left_outer_joins(board: :entropy)
          .joins("LEFT OUTER JOIN entropies AS account_entropies ON account_entropies.account_id = accounts.id AND account_entropies.container_type = 'Account' AND account_entropies.container_id = accounts.id")
          .where("cards.last_active_at <= #{connection.date_subtract('?', 'COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period)')}", now)
      else
        none
      end
    end

    scope :postponing_soon, -> do
      now = Time.now
      min_period, max_period = Entropy.pick(Arel.sql("MIN(auto_postpone_period), MAX(auto_postpone_period)"))

      if min_period && max_period
        published
          .where(last_active_at: (now - max_period - 1.second)..(now - min_period * 0.75 + 1.second))
          .where("NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM closures WHERE closures.card_id = cards.id)")
          .where("NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM card_not_nows WHERE card_not_nows.card_id = cards.id)")
          .joins(board: :account)
          .left_outer_joins(board: :entropy)
          .joins("LEFT OUTER JOIN entropies AS account_entropies ON account_entropies.account_id = accounts.id AND account_entropies.container_type = 'Account' AND account_entropies.container_id = accounts.id")
          .where("cards.last_active_at > #{connection.date_subtract('?', 'COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period)')}", now)
          .where("cards.last_active_at <= #{connection.date_subtract('?', 'COALESCE(entropies.auto_postpone_period, account_entropies.auto_postpone_period) * 0.75')}", now)
      else
        none
      end
    end

    delegate :auto_postpone_period, to: :board
  end

  class_methods do
    def auto_postpone_all_due
      system_users = {}

      due_to_be_postponed.pluck(:id).each_slice(1000) do |batch_ids|
        where(id: batch_ids).each do |card|
          system_user = system_users[card.account_id] ||= card.account.system_user
          card.auto_postpone(user: system_user)
        end
      end
    end
  end

  def entropy
    Card::Entropy.for(self)
  end

  def entropic?
    entropy.present?
  end
end
EOF

  setup do

    cards(:layout).update! last_active_at: 2.day.ago
    assert_equal (90 - 2).days.from_now, cards(:layout).entropy.auto_clean_at
  end

    account_entropy = entropies("37s_account")
    original_period = account_entropy.auto_postpone_period

    entropies(:writebook_board).destroy
    boards(:writebook).update! auto_postpone_period: 365.days

require "test_helper"

class Card::EntropicTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  setup do
    Current.session = sessions(:david)
  end

  test "auto_postpone_at uses the period defined in the account by default" do
    freeze_time

    entropies(:writebook_board).destroy
    entropies("37s_account").reload.update! auto_postpone_period: 365.days
    cards(:layout).update! last_active_at: 2.day.ago
    assert_equal (365 - 2).days.from_now, cards(:layout).entropy.auto_clean_at
  end

  test "auto_postpone_at infers the period from the board when present" do
    freeze_time

    entropies(:writebook_board).update! auto_postpone_period: 90.days
    cards(:layout).update! last_active_at: 2.day.ago
    assert_equal (90 - 2).days.from_now, cards(:layout).entropy.auto_clean_at
  end

  test "setting auto_postpone_period in the board without entropy will create it, without affecting the account entropy" do
    account_entropy = entropies("37s_account")
    original_period = account_entropy.auto_postpone_period

    entropies(:writebook_board).destroy
    boards(:writebook).update! auto_postpone_period: 365.days

    assert_equal original_period, account_entropy.reload.auto_postpone_period
  end

  test "auto postpone all due using the default account entropy" do
    entropies(:writebook_board).destroy

    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: 1.day.ago - entropies("37s_account").auto_postpone_period)
    cards(:shipping).update!(last_active_at: 1.day.from_now - entropies("37s_account").auto_postpone_period)

    assert_difference -> { Card.postponed.count }, +1 do
      Card.auto_postpone_all_due
    end

    assert cards(:logo).reload.postponed?
    assert_equal accounts("37s").system_user, cards(:logo).postponed_by
    assert_not cards(:shipping).reload.postponed?\
  end

  test "auto postpone all due using entropy defined at the board level" do
    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: 1.day.ago - entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period)
    cards(:shipping).update!(last_active_at: 1.day.from_now - entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period)

    assert_difference -> { Card.postponed.count }, +1 do
      Card.auto_postpone_all_due
    end

    assert cards(:logo).reload.postponed?
    assert_not cards(:shipping).reload.postponed?
  end

  test "postponing soon scope" do
    cards(:logo, :shipping).each(&:published!)

    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago + 2.days)
    cards(:shipping).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago - 2.days)

    assert_includes Card.postponing_soon, cards(:logo)
    assert_not_includes Card.postponing_soon, cards(:shipping)
  end

  test "auto postpone all due works properly cross-account" do
    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago - 2.days)
    cards(:radio).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:miltons_wish_list_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago - 2.days)

    Card.auto_postpone_all_due

    assert cards(:logo).reload.postponed?
    assert cards(:radio).reload.postponed?
  end

  test "postponing_soon scope works properly cross-account" do
    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:writebook_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago + 2.days)
    cards(:radio).update!(last_active_at: entropies(:miltons_wish_list_board).auto_postpone_period.seconds.ago + 2.days)

    assert_equal(cards(:logo, :radio).to_set, Card.postponing_soon.to_set)
  end

  test "due_to_be_postponed and auto_postpone_all_due ignore drafted, closed, and already postponed cards" do
    old_time = 2.years.ago

    drafted_card = cards(:logo)
    drafted_card.update!(status: :drafted, last_active_at: old_time)

    closed_card = cards(:layout)
    closed_card.close
    closed_card.update!(last_active_at: old_time)

    postponed_card = cards(:text)
    postponed_card.postpone
    postponed_card.update!(last_active_at: old_time)

    due_card = cards(:shipping)
    due_card.update!(last_active_at: old_time)

    assert_equal [ due_card ], Card.due_to_be_postponed.to_a
    assert_empty Card.postponing_soon

    assert_difference -> { Card.postponed.count }, +1 do
      Card.auto_postpone_all_due
    end

    assert due_card.reload.postponed?
    assert_not drafted_card.reload.postponed?
    assert closed_card.reload.closed?
    assert postponed_card.reload.postponed?
  end

  test "due_to_be_postponed respects mixed periods across boards" do
    entropies(:writebook_board).update!(auto_postpone_period: 365.days)
    entropies(:miltons_wish_list_board).update!(auto_postpone_period: 3.days)

    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: 60.days.ago)
    cards(:radio).update!(last_active_at: 4.days.ago)

    assert_not_includes Card.due_to_be_postponed, cards(:logo)
    assert_includes Card.due_to_be_postponed, cards(:radio)

    Card.auto_postpone_all_due

    assert_not cards(:logo).reload.postponed?
    assert cards(:radio).reload.postponed?
  end

  test "due_to_be_postponed and postponing_soon return empty when no entropies exist" do
    cards(:logo).update!(last_active_at: 2.years.ago)
    Entropy.delete_all

    assert_empty Card.due_to_be_postponed
    assert_empty Card.postponing_soon
    assert_no_difference -> { Card.postponed.count } do
      Card.auto_postpone_all_due
    end
  end
end
